document.title: Motion for Leave to Answer and Answer of Geronimo Power, LLC to the answer of Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. filed on 11/09/2026
document.group: MISO Large Load Addition Resource Study (LARS)

pages.text:
UNITED STATES OF AMERICA 
BEFORE THE 
FEDERAL ENERGY REGULATORY COMMISSION 
Midcontinent Independent System  
Operator, Inc. 
) 
) 
) 
) 
 
Docket No. ER27-25-000 
 
 
MOTION FOR LEAVE TO ANSWER AND ANSWER OF  
GERONIMO POWER, LLC 
 
Pursuant to Rules 212 and 213 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“FERC” 
or “Commission”) Rules of Practice and Procedure,1 Geronimo Power, LLC (“Geronimo Power”) 
hereby moves for leave to answer2 and files this answer to the answer3 of the Midcontinent 
Independent System Operator, Inc. (“MISO”) regarding its Large Load Addition Resource Study 
Process (“LARS”) proposal.4 
I. 
ANSWER 
Geronimo Power agrees with MISO’s assessment that the significant load growth that 
MISO is experiencing requires MISO to adopt new processes to integrate new large loads and 
serve their demand.5  Geronimo Power’s comments in this proceeding commended MISO for its 
 
1 18 C.F.R. §§ 385.212 and 385.213. 
2 Geronimo Power acknowledges that the Commission’s Rules of Practice and Procedure do not typically 
allow answers to answers.  However, the Commission has accepted answers in the past when they have (i) assisted 
the Commission in understanding the issues presented, (ii) provided additional information for the Commission’s 
decision-making process, and (iii) helped ensure a complete and accurate record.  See, e.g., PJM Interconnection, 
L.L.C., 181 FERC ¶ 61,162, at P 29 (2022); Canal Generating LLC, 181 FERC ¶ 61,157, at P 14 (2022); Equitrans, 
L.P., 134 FERC ¶ 61,250, at P 6 (2011); Cal. Indep. Sys. Operator Corp., 132 FERC ¶ 61,023, at P 16 (2010).  In this 
proceeding, Geronimo Power’s answer will help the Commission understand the issues presented by MISO’s filing 
and provide further information related to the issues in this proceeding to inform the Commission’s decision-making 
process.  Geronimo Power therefore respectfully requests leave to file this answer and asks the Commission to consider 
this answer in its deliberations in this proceeding. 
3 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER27-25-000, Motion for Leave to Answer and 
Answer of the Midcontinent Independent System Operator, Inc. (Nov. 9, 2026) (“MISO Answer”).  
4 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER27-25-000, Large Load Addition Resource Study 
Process (Oct. 2, 2026) (“LARS Filing”).  
5 MISO Answer at 3.

2 
 
efforts to address this challenge, but raised critical questions regarding whether MISO’s proposed 
LARS process would in fact achieve MISO’s goals while remaining consistent with open access 
principles.6  MISO’s Answer fails to meaningfully respond to the concerns raised by Geronimo 
Power.  Accordingly, Geronimo Power urges the Commission to reject LARS without prejudice 
to MISO submitting a revised proposal that addresses the significant issues identified by Geronimo 
Power and other parties in this proceeding. 
A. 
MISO Has Not Addressed The Arbitrary And Unduly Discriminatory 
Limitations LARS Places On Eligible Agreements And Co-Location 
Arrangements 
 
Geronimo Power demonstrated that the current design of LARS appears to limit the use of 
this process by large loads and generation resources that are pursuing certain supply arrangements 
that support resource adequacy and protect ratepayers.  For instance, Geronimo Power noted that 
MISO’s proposed tariff language appears to preclude interconnection customers that have entered 
into a virtual power purchase agreement (“PPA”) from submitting an application into the LARS 
process.7  Geronimo Power’s comments also questioned whether co-location arrangements would 
be eligible for LARS given MISO’s statements suggesting that co-location arrangements could 
only be pursued through MISO’s Zero Injection Generator Interconnection Agreement 
framework.8  MISO’s Answer provides no response or clarification to these issues.    
The only response offered in MISO’s Answer is a generic assertion that the agreement 
requirement is “flexible enough for projects with commercial certainty to participate” and that the 
“agreement requirement should not be made more flexible to allow in projects that do not meet the 
 
6 Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., Docket No. ER27-25-000, Motion to Intervene and Comments of 
Geronimo Power, LLC at 2-5 (Oct. 23, 2026) (“Geronimo Comments”). 
7 Id. at 14-16. 
8 Id. at 16-17.

3 
 
high hurdle that LARS is designed to maintain.”9  But Geronimo Power is not arguing for MISO 
to relax its standards.  A long-term virtual PPA provides the same level of commercial certainty 
as a long-term physical PPA and allowing this arrangement to qualify for LARS would in no way 
lower the bar MISO has set.  MISO’s restrictions on virtual PPAs and other supply arrangements 
arbitrarily prevent customers that are pursuing supply arrangements that are consistent with the 
objectives underlying LARS and the Show Cause Order from accessing the LARS process.10  
Virtual PPAs increasingly are being used by large loads to support the construction of the 
new generation needed to meet their demand.11  Virtual PPAs accomplish exactly what MISO says 
LARS is intended to encourage: they de-risk new generation, support the entry of the capacity 
needed to offset the resource adequacy requirements of new large loads, and place the cost of 
resources on the large loads they will serve rather than on retail customers.12  Indeed, MISO’s own 
explanation of LARS confirms that allowing physical PPAs to qualify for LARS while excluding 
virtual PPAs makes little sense.  Specifically, MISO concedes that LARS does not require the 
 
9 MISO Answer at 25. 
10 See Midcontinent Indep. Sys. Operator, Inc., 195 FERC ¶ 61,212, at P 113 (2026) (“Show Cause Order”). 
11 See, e.g., Zachary Skidmore, Google Signs vPPA with Cypress Creek for 2.45 GW Solar Project in 
Arkansas – Report, Data Center Dynamics (July 14, 2026), https://www.datacenterdynamics.com/en/news/google-
signs-vppa-with-cypress-creek-for-245gw-solar-project-in-arkansas-report (reporting that Google signed a long-term 
virtual PPA for the full output of the Steel River Energy Center, a 2.45 GW solar plus storage facility in Mississippi 
County, Arkansas and that the revenue commitment allowed the developer “to commence construction of the 
project”); EDP Global, EDP Renewables North America Delivers Three Additional Renewable Energy Projects for 
Microsoft (Feb. 10, 2025), https://edp.com/en/north-america/na/media/edp-renewables-north-america-delivers-three-
additional-renewable-energy (noting that Microsoft “agreed to purchase 389 MW of electricity and renewable energy 
credits (RECs) from the projects [in Illinois and Texas] through long-term virtual power purchase agreements 
(VPPAs)”); Sustainability Roundtable, Inc., Akamai Technologies, Teradyne, and Wayfair Partner to Purchase Solar 
Energy in Champaign County, Ill. Through the Net Zero Consortium for Buyers, GlobeNewswire (Sept. 26, 2024), 
https://www.globenewswire.com/news-release/2024/09/26/2953870/0/en/Akamai-Technologies-Teradyne-and-
Wayfair-Partner-to-Purchase-Solar-Energy-in-Champaign-County-Ill-Through-the-Net-Zero-Consortium-for-
Buyers.html (describing an “aggregated virtual power purchase agreement” for the 135 MWac Prairie Solar project in 
development in the MISO region of Illinois).  See also Brian Martucci, Meta-Constellation virtual PPA could be first 
of 
many 
deals 
for 
existing 
reactor 
output: 
experts, 
UtilityDive 
(June 
12, 
2025), 
https://www.utilitydive.com/news/meta-constellation-ppa-could-be-first-of-many-deals-for-existing-
reactors/750567/. 
12 Geronimo Comments at 15-16.

4 
 
output of the generating facility to match the demand of load because that “is not the mechanism 
LARS uses to create value and potential savings.”13  If the physical delivery of energy to the load 
is irrelevant to the goal LARS is intended to achieve, there is no basis for excluding resources that 
are financially, rather than physically, committed to serving that load.  And while load-serving 
entities (“LSE”) and Alternative Retail Electric Suppliers have the option of obtaining LARS 
eligibility through “other types of agreements” that would allow for a wider range of commercial 
arrangements, this option is not available to independent power producers (“IPP”) and large 
loads14—a distinction that is unduly discriminatory and for which MISO has failed to provide any 
justification. 
  MISO has similarly failed to justify excluding co-located load and generation from the 
LARS process.  Co-located load and generation supported by a long-term PPA or similar 
arrangement are similarly situated to electrically proximate pairs in every respect relevant to 
LARS: both pairings are based on a binding agreement between the two entities, are located in the 
same local resource zone, are studied together for their combined system impacts, and are intended 
to bring new generation online to serve a specific load.15  Indeed, co-location arrangements are 
better situated to achieve the goals of LARS because they are less likely to trigger transmission 
upgrades relative to generation that is merely “electrically proximate” to the load.  And the 
Commission’s Show Cause Order also made no distinction between these two arrangements.16  Yet 
MISO has refused to clarify that co-located load and generation will be eligible for LARS. 
 
13 MISO Answer at 10.  See also id. at 24 (“MISO is not requiring a generating facility’s output to be matched 
to the demand of the electrically proximate large load.”). 
14 LARS Filing, Proposed Tariff, Att. X § 3.12.2(i)(c); LARS Filing, Tab C, Prepared Direct Testimony of 
Christina Drake at 31-32. 
15 See Geronimo Comments at 17-18 (citing Show Cause Order at P 113).  
16 Id. at 16-18.

5 
 
MISO does not dispute Geronimo Power’s arguments that there is no reason to exclude co-
location arrangements from LARS.  In fact, MISO concedes that “adjacent large loads and 
Generating Facilities may produce the most significant Network Upgrade optimization” and touts 
LARS as an “electrically proximate plus” construct that encourages generation and load to site “as 
close together as is practical.”17  Despite these concessions, MISO has offered no clarification that 
co-location arrangements are eligible for LARS.  MISO should not be permitted to design LARS 
around the electrical proximity of load and generation and then exclude the very pairings that have 
the closest electrical proximity and that it acknowledges will produce the greatest benefits.  
B. 
MISO’s Answer Fails To Meaningfully Address The Unduly Discriminatory 
Components Of LARS  
 
Under the LARS process, a generation resource may enter into an agreement to serve a 
large load and otherwise meet all the criteria to participate in LARS but will nevertheless be 
ineligible unless a transmission customer—which MISO concedes will often be an LSE—agrees 
to submit a LARS application on its behalf.18  Moreover, this same generation resource and large 
load pairing will be ineligible for the LARS process unless the transmission owner of the system 
they are interconnecting to agrees to a proposed point of interconnection.19  These components of 
LARS effectively give incumbent utilities, in the form of LSEs and transmission owners, the 
ability to prevent otherwise viable generation and load pairings from accessing LARS. 
Although MISO says that it disagrees with commenters’ characterization of the LARS 
process as placing LSEs in a gatekeeper role,20 it does not offer any arguments or evidence to rebut 
commenters’ characterization.  MISO instead defends the gatekeeping role LSEs and transmission 
 
17 MISO Answer at 11-12. 
18 LARS Filing, Transmittal Letter at 6.  
19 Id. at 8. 
20 MISO Answer at 20.

6 
 
owners will be permitted to play in the LARS process on the grounds that, like its Expedited Project 
Review process, “LARS is a load-driven process, and an Interconnection Customer cannot require 
a Transmission Customer to scope their Transmission Service request around a generator they have 
not chosen to pair with.”21  MISO’s defense is flawed for numerous reasons. 
To begin with, MISO’s argument on this point is circular.  To the extent that LARS is a 
load-driven process, that is only because MISO designed it as such.  It does not, however, absolve 
MISO of its obligation to demonstrate that the process it has designed is consistent with the Federal 
Power Act’s (“FPA”) prohibition on undue discrimination.  Indeed, if MISO’s rationale were to 
hold, public utilities would be permitted to adopt any unduly discriminatory interconnection 
policies so long as the design of the policies was intended to accomplish the utilities’ stated goals.   
MISO similarly dismisses the fact that Southwest Power Pool, Inc.’s (“SPP”) High Impact 
Large Load Generation Assessment (“HILLGA”) process provides generation resources with a 
non-discriminatory pathway to interconnect and serve electrically proximate large loads on the 
grounds that it is a “generator-driven process.”22  But MISO’s claim that LARS is a load-driven 
process ignores that LARS is not simply a load study; it is also a generator interconnection process 
that results in a resource obtaining a Large Load Generator Interconnection Agreement (“LLGIA”) 
and Network Resource Interconnection Service.23  Indeed, the key components of LARS are 
focused on the interconnection of a generation resource and the interconnection customer’s 
resulting interconnection rights.  MISO’s own filing, for instance, defines a LARS Application as 
“a form of Interconnection Request.”24  And under MISO’s proposal, the interconnection 
 
21 Id.  
22 Id. at 21. 
23 LARS Filing, Tab C, Prepared Direct Testimony of Christina Drake at 12-13; id., Transmittal Letter at 6. 
24 Id., Transmittal Letter at 7, n.29.

7 
 
customer—not the transmission customer or transmission owner—completes the generation 
portion of the application, satisfies the Attachment X requirements, posts the required security, 
executes the LLGIA, and bears responsibility for network upgrades.25  In contrast, MISO’s filing 
is largely devoid of explanation as to how a transmission customer is to obtain transmission service 
for a LARS Associated Load.    
Even if the LARS process were accurately characterized as a load-driven process, MISO 
fails to justify requiring a commercially viable large load and its paired generation resource to 
obtain the support and consent of LSEs and transmission owners to access the process.  MISO 
asserts that so long as an interconnection customer and load can obtain the agreement of a 
transmission customer to initiate the LARS application, there is no barrier to them entering the 
LARS process and without such agreement “the pairing of load and generation in a coordinated 
study process would be premature and speculative.”26  MISO does not explain, however, why the 
ability of a generation resource to obtain the agreement of an incumbent utility to submit an 
application is a reasonable benchmark for commercial viability.  A generation developer only 
would be able to enter LARS if it has an executed long-term agreement with the entity that owns 
or controls the LARS Associated Load or the LARS Associated Transmission Customer already, 
100% site control, and deposits in hand.  These measures already are sufficient to deter speculative 
requests and ensure the commercial viability of a proposed resource.  Requiring a generation 
developer and large load to obtain the agreement of the incumbent utility to submit the LARS 
 
25 MISO has also failed to address discrepancies in its tariff that create ambiguity regarding the entity that is 
eligible to submit a LARS Application.  As Geronimo Power explained in its comments, although MISO states that a 
LARS Application may only be initiated by the LARS Associated Transmission Customer, proposed Section 3.12.1 
of Attachment X states that “[p]rior to the applicable Transmission Owner submitting a LARS Application, the 
potential LARS Interconnection Customer and the Transmission Owner shall meet and agree on a definitive Point of 
Interconnection for the LARS Generating Facility.”  Geronimo Comments at 7, n.16 (emphasis added).  MISO’s 
Answer fails to clarify that the LARS Associated Transmission Customer is responsible for submitting the LARS 
application rather than the transmission owner.  
26 MISO Answer at 20.

8 
 
application merely creates opportunities for undue discrimination that incumbent utilities can use 
to create barriers to entry without any corresponding benefit.  
MISO’s defense of the requirement that the transmission owner pre-approve a project’s 
point of interconnection before a LARS application may be submitted is equally unsupported.  
MISO states that LARS “has stricter site control requirements such that the Transmission Owner 
must agree on the POI at the time of application submission” to ensure that only shovel-ready 
projects participate.27  But site control and a transmission owner veto are different things.  An 
interconnection customer can demonstrate site control and identify a point of interconnection 
without having to await the interconnecting transmission owner’s approval.  Indeed, in the 
generator interconnection context, no transmission owner consent to a point of interconnection is 
required, yet evidence of site control is still provided.28  And requiring transmission owner 
approval also does not provide meaningful protection against the risk that technical issues could 
arise that could lead the transmission owner or MISO to request a change in the point of 
interconnection during the study process.29 
MISO also does not demonstrate that it is just and reasonable to require interconnection 
customers to bear the risk of a transmission owner-initiated change to the point of interconnection 
that occurs during the study process.  As Geronimo Power pointed out in its comments, MISO’s 
proposal not only requires the transmission owner to agree to the point of interconnection in order 
for a customer to enter the LARS process, but proposes language that would deem a customer’s 
request withdrawn if the transmission owner later changes its mind and proposes to modify the 
 
27 Id. at 21. 
28 See MISO Tariff, Att. X § 7.2.1(ii).  
29 Geronimo Comments at 12-13.

9 
 
point of interconnection.30  The result is that the transmission owner holds not only an up-front 
veto over a project’s entry into LARS but also a continuing ability to remove the project from the 
process after the fact, and MISO offers no justification for placing the consequences of that 
unilateral decision on the interconnection customer rather than on the party that made it. 
Ultimately, MISO’s defense of the gatekeeping role that LSEs and transmission owners 
will be permitted to play for LARS appears to hinge on a fundamental misunderstanding of the 
FPA’s prohibition on undue discrimination and the Commission’s open access principles.  MISO 
appears to believe that so long as its proposal does not expressly prohibit IPPs from accessing 
LARS, it is not unduly discriminatory.31  But that is not how courts or the Commission evaluate 
whether a proposal is unduly discriminatory and consistent with open access.  The Commission 
has repeatedly rejected proposals that provide the mere opportunity for undue discrimination by 
incumbent utilities.32  Moreover, whether a proposal is facially neutral—as MISO claims LARS 
is—has no bearing on whether its effect is unduly discriminatory and unlawful under the FPA.33   
 
30 Id. at 13, n.31 (citing LARS Filing, Proposed Tariff, Att. X § 3.12.9). 
31 MISO Answer at 20 (“LARS does not prevent Independent Power Producers (‘IPPs’) from competing to 
supply energy to large loads under applicable state and or [sic] utility-led RFP processes.”).  See also id. at 22 (“If an 
IPP has a generation project that is better, more cost effective, or otherwise preferable to alternatives, nothing in the 
LARS process stops the IPP from bringing this project forward for consideration and entering into a pairing 
arrangement with a LARS Transmission Customer.”). 
32 Standardization of Generator Interconnection Agreements and Procedures, Order No. 2003, 104 FERC ¶ 
61,103, at PP 11, 696 (2003), order on reh’g, Order No. 2003‐A, 106 FERC ¶ 61,220 (2004), order on reh’g, Order 
No. 2003‐B, 109 FERC ¶ 61,287 (2005), order on reh’g, Order No. 2003‐C, 111 FERC ¶ 61,401 (2005), aff’d sub 
nom., National Ass’n of Regulatory Util. Comm’rs v. FERC, 475 F.3d 1277 (D.C. Cir. 2007) (“The Commission would 
find any policy that creates opportunities for such discriminatory behavior to be unacceptable.”). 
33 See Xcel Energy Servs. v. FERC, 41 F.4th 548, 559-60 (D.C. Cir. 2022) (quoting Pub. Serv. Co. of Colo., 
172 FERC ¶ 61,297, at P 13 (2020)).

10 
 
II. 
CONCLUSION 
Geronimo Power respectfully requests that the Commission issue an order consistent with 
its filings in this proceeding and reject LARS without prejudice to MISO submitting a revised 
proposal that addresses the significant issues identified by Geronimo Power and other parties in 
this proceeding.  
Respectfully submitted,
